headline: Massachusetts awards nearly $40M in life-science tax incentives tied to 1,644 jobs
dek: The awards span 38 companies, with most of the expected new positions located outside Boston and Cambridge and commitments subject to three years of reporting.
body: Massachusetts has awarded nearly $40 million in tax incentives to 38 life-science companies that collectively pledged to create 1,644 new jobs, putting a statewide economic-development program behind expansions in research, therapeutics, diagnostics and manufacturing. Gov. Maura Healey announced the awards Sept. 28 at SMC Ltd. in Devens. The figures describe company commitments, not jobs already filled or money paid directly to workers. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs)

The geographic distribution is a central feature of this round. The Massachusetts Life Sciences Center said 31 of the 38 awardees are expanding outside Boston and Cambridge, and those projects account for 71% of the expected new jobs. That puts communities such as Acton, Andover, Bedford, Burlington, Chelmsford, Devens, Framingham, Marlborough, Milford, Northbridge, Sudbury, Waltham and Woburn in the direct path of the announced hiring commitments, rather than limiting the benefit to the state's traditional laboratory hubs. The agency described the program as a way to use Massachusetts' broader network of life-science assets for growth and retention. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs)

The largest individual award goes to Acton-based Insulet Corporation: $10 million tied to a 250-job commitment. Lila Sciences in Cambridge received $3.6 million for 200 jobs, while Vertex Pharmaceuticals in Boston received $3.025 million for 121 jobs. Other sizable awards include $2.875 million for Bristol Myers Squibb's 125-job commitment in Devens, $1.86 million for TransMedics in Andover, and $1.35 million for SMC's 54 jobs in Devens. The Boston Business Journal reported that the full list also includes AstraZeneca, Vericel, Zoll Medical, Rentschler Biopharma and dozens of smaller firms. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html)

The awards are tax incentives administered through the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center's Tax Incentive Program jointly with the Department of Revenue. The program is open to companies doing research and development, commercialization or manufacturing in Massachusetts, and the commitments are meant to be new, long-term positions. Awardees must maintain their job commitments for three years and file regular reports documenting the jobs created as a result of the incentives. That structure makes the announced 1,644 jobs a measurable target that can be checked over time, rather than an immediate headcount. The state release also says the program has supported commitments for more than 22,300 jobs since the center was established. (https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-announces-40-million-to-grow-massachusetts-life-sciences-industry-create-more-than-1600-jobs)

Demand for the program was stronger than the award total. The Boston Business Journal reported that companies submitted $58 million in applications this year, compared with a previous year when the center needed two rounds to allocate the full $40 million authorization. The outlet also reported that, since 2009, the center has made 519 awards to nearly 300 distinct companies totaling about $422 million and tied to more than 22,300 jobs. Those figures show both the scale of the state's strategy and the competitive choices behind this year's list: the program is not an open-ended subsidy for every applicant, and some proposals were not funded in this cycle. (https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/news/2026/09/28/mass-tax-incentive-program-2026.html)

The current ceiling comes from the 2024 Mass Leads Act, which raised the annual statutory cap for life-science tax incentives from $30 million to $40 million and broadened the eligible field to include areas such as medical technology, preventative medicine, biosecurity and life-science-related artificial intelligence. Massachusetts' technical tax guidance describes the program as a collection of tax incentives available to qualifying companies, rather than a single grant pot. That distinction matters when evaluating the public return: the state is trading foregone tax revenue for promised hiring and investment, while the companies still have to execute their expansion plans. (https://www.mass.gov/technical-information-release/tir-25-5-tax-provisions-in-certain-massachusetts-legislation-enacted-in-2024)

For workers and municipalities, the next test is delivery. Companies must meet the hiring and retention conditions attached to their awards, and the state must report whether projects translate into sustained employment across the Commonwealth. The announcement includes activity in artificial intelligence, women's health, therapeutics, diagnostics, medical technology, research and development and biomanufacturing. If the commitments hold, the round will distribute new positions across a wider geography and reinforce Massachusetts' life-science supply chain; if projects fall short, the reporting and tax-administration process will determine how the state responds. The award announcement establishes the targets, but future compliance records will show how many jobs actually materialize.
author: NorthEast News Desk
